title: China's Economy Grows at Slowest Pace Since 2022 as Investment Plunges
excerpt: GDP expanded just 4.3% in the second quarter, missing Beijing's own target range as fixed-asset investment fell 5.7% and the property sector contracted further.
body:
• China's Q2 GDP grew 4.3% year-on-year, the weakest pace since Q4 2022 and below the 4.5% consensus forecast.
  • Fixed-asset investment contracted 5.7% in the first half, while property investment plunged 18%, deepening the structural imbalance between exports and domestic demand.
  • Exports surged 27% in June, driven by AI hardware and green-tech shipments, masking severe weakness in household consumption.
  • India's bilateral trade with China reached $91.72 billion in H1 2026, with Indian exports to China rising 37.2% — but the trade deficit widened to $67.1 billion.

China's economy expanded at its slowest rate in more than three years during the April–June quarter, with collapsing domestic investment overwhelming a strong export performance and intensifying pressure on Beijing to deploy fresh stimulus measures.

Gross domestic product grew 4.3% year-on-year in Q2, down sharply from 5.0% in the first quarter, according to data released by China's National Bureau of Statistics on July 15. The reading missed the median analyst forecast of 4.5% compiled by Reuters and fell below the lower bound of Beijing's 4.5%–5.0% full-year growth target — the first such miss since the pandemic era.

On a quarter-on-quarter basis, the economy expanded 0.9%, decelerating from 1.3% in January–March.

Investment Collapse Drags Growth

The primary drag came from a broad-based downturn in investment. Fixed-asset investment shrank 5.7% year-on-year in January–June, with even state-sector investment declining 2.3%. Property investment cratered 18%, extending a slide that has persisted since 2021 and continues to erode household wealth across the country.

"It's really the worst data possible for investment," said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at Natixis. "With infrastructure saving the day, it's really not enough."

Local governments, long the primary drivers of infrastructure and manufacturing investment, are now under pressure to rein in spending as ballooning debt obligations consume their budgets. Li Daokui, an economics professor at Tsinghua University, identified the fiscal retreat of local governments as "the single biggest factor behind the current cooling of China's economy."

Consumers Pull Back

Household consumption offered little relief. Retail sales rose just 1.0% in June, a marginal rebound from May's outright decline — the first negative reading since December 2022. Wages have stagnated or fallen in several sectors, while the prolonged property downturn has diminished household wealth and sentiment.

Industrial overcapacity, U.S. tariffs, and price wars among domestic producers have fuelled layoffs in manufacturing, according to Reuters. Meanwhile, faster AI adoption has slowed white-collar job creation, pushing tens of millions of workers into the gig economy with lower pay and weaker social protections.

Exports — the Lone Bright Spot

China's exports surged 27% in June, buoyed by the global AI boom and frontloading by U.S. retailers securing inventory ahead of potential tariff increases. Semiconductors, computer parts, and power equipment accounted for roughly half of export growth in the first half, according to Macquarie Group research.

The Iran war has inadvertently bolstered demand for Chinese clean-energy products. Monthly car exports exceeded one million units for the first time in June as oil-dependent economies accelerated their shift to electric vehicles and solar panels.

But analysts warn that heavy reliance on external demand leaves China vulnerable. "What will cause the current situation to change is when exports fail," said Larry Hu, Macquarie's chief China economist. "When exports slow down, the government will do more on domestic demand."

Stimulus Expectations and Policy Signals

The weak data has put a late-July Politburo meeting squarely in focus. Beijing plans to spend 7 trillion yuan ($1 trillion) this year on national infrastructure projects spanning water networks, power grids, and computing centres, according to state media. Changjiang Securities estimates such investment could total 26.9 trillion yuan over five years.

Yet analysts remain skeptical of a major fiscal pivot. Zhiwei Zhang, chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said the government appears "reluctant to spend fiscal resources and build up debt" while exports hold. Morgan Stanley and ANZ both cut their full-year GDP forecasts to 4.6% following the Q2 miss.

"No domestic demand, all about exports — it's really quite unsustainable, to be frank."

— Alicia Garcia-Herrero, Chief Economist for Asia Pacific, Natixis

What It Means for India

China's slowdown carries direct implications for India and its diaspora. Bilateral trade reached $91.72 billion in the first half of 2026, with India's exports to China surging 37.2% to $12.31 billion, according to Chinese customs data reported by The Economic Times. However, India's trade deficit with China widened to $67.1 billion.

Indian policymakers and exporters are watching for two risks: Chinese manufacturers dumping excess production into the Indian market as domestic demand falters, and a potential reversal in AI-driven exports that could disrupt supply chains for Indian technology firms sourcing components from China. The IMF has maintained its forecast of 6.4% growth for India in FY27, noting the country remains the world's fastest-growing major economy.
